cards.explanation: The potter is working at his wheel. Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, goes down and finds him "…working at the wheel." (Jeremiah 18:3) The LORD had told him to go there, and that He would give His message at the potter's house (Jeremiah 18:2). I think this is a scene where you simply watch and learn. Sometimes the best classroom is somebody else's workshop.

The potter forms the clay into another vessel. The verse says “so he formed it into another vessel, as it seemed best for him to do.” (Jeremiah 18:4) The flaw doesn't end the clay's story, friends. The potter just keeps going with the same lump and a new plan.

The answer is True. The LORD says, “Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel.” (Jeremiah 18:6) Israel is the clay, and the LORD is the potter holding it. That's the picture Jeremiah just watched at the wheel.

The answer is False. Here's what the text says: “But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring.” (Jeremiah 18:8) The warning comes with a way out. When a nation turns, the disaster doesn't come as planned.

The answer is that He will relent of it. The LORD says, “…then I will relent of the good I had intended for it.” (Jeremiah 18:10) This is the same teaching as before, just flipped. How a nation responds to Him matters, in both directions.

The LORD tells each of them to turn from their evil ways. He says, “Turn now, each of you, from your evil ways, and correct your ways and deeds.” (Jeremiah 18:11) Notice it's "…each of you…" so it's personal, not just a crowd move. The warning and the invitation come in the same breath.

The answer is False. The LORD says they will reply, “It is hopeless. We will follow our own plans, and each of us will act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.” (Jeremiah 18:12) That's not a promise to turn, it's a refusal. After a call like the one in verse 11, that one stings.

The word is forgotten. The LORD says, “Yet My people have forgotten Me.” (Jeremiah 18:15) Lebanon's snow and cool waters stay where they belong, and that makes the contrast hit. I think that's the point of the picture: some things you can count on, and His people didn't stay put like that.

They are walking on rutted bypaths off the highway. The LORD says they're “…leaving the ancient roads to walk on rutted bypaths instead of on the highway.” (Jeremiah 18:15) Rutted bypaths sound bumpy to me, bakers. Think of rolling dough across a counter covered in crumbs. Nothing comes out smooth.

The answer is True. The LORD says the land will be a desolation, and “all who pass by will be appalled and shake their heads.” (Jeremiah 18:16) Everybody passing by gets the same reaction. That's a lot of head shaking, if you ask me.

He will show them His back and not His face. The LORD says, “I will show them My back and not My face in the day of their calamity.” (Jeremiah 18:17) I think this is one of the heavy parts of the chapter. It's a hard thing to read, so let's let it be hard.

They decide to denounce him and ignore his words. Some people say, “Come, let us denounce him and pay no heed to any of his words.” (Jeremiah 18:18) The "him" is Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet. It's like muting a group chat so you never have to read what's in it.
The word is evil. Jeremiah asks, “Should good be repaid with evil?” (Jeremiah 18:20) I think that one hurts. It's the question of someone who tried to help and got a trap in return.

Jeremiah spoke up on their behalf. He tells the LORD, “Remember how I stood before You to speak good on their behalf, to turn Your wrath from them.” (Jeremiah 18:20) He stood in front of the LORD for the very people now plotting against him. No wonder he's asking if good gets repaid with evil.

The answer is True. Jeremiah says, “…for they have dug a pit to capture me and have hidden snares for my feet.” (Jeremiah 18:22) That's a pit and snares both. I think he's laying the whole picture out for the LORD.

The answer is False. Jeremiah prays, “Do not wipe out their guilt or blot out their sin from Your sight.” (Jeremiah 18:23) That's the reverse of asking for it to be wiped out. It's a heavy prayer, and I think it shows how much he's hurting.
